results.title: Tariffs send shockwaves through Georgia's industries
results.content:
Chinese tariffs could especially affect local businesses, the Georgia chamber noted. China was the third largest buyer of local goods last year at $3 billion, behind Canada and Mexico, and the second highest importer to Georgia at $17.2 billion.

On April 3, the chamber published a report outlining the impacts local industries may experience from the tariffs, including higher prices for car parts and steel, a squeeze on crop imports and possible slowdowns at the state’s bustling ports. [...] Remaining in effect, thus far, are a 25% tariff on imported cars and car parts and a 125% tariff on all Chinese goods — both of which, observers say, could deal an immediate blow to Georgia industries.

image description

### Car parts chaos

Not all industries are feeling as optimistic as the chamber about the sudden tariff change. [...] The White House initially established 10% tariffs on imports from all countries, along with higher “reciprocal” tariffs targeting nations such as China, Vietnam and members of the European Union that levy tariffs on U.S. goods. Mexico and Canada — Georgia’s top export destinations — were spared from the new tariffs.

results.title: How a trade war could move American EVs out of reach
results.content:
Hyundai officially opened its huge new EV factory in Georgia last month. Last week, the startup Sila began commissioning its first factory in Washington state to make silicon anodes, a new kind of battery component where China has no advantage. And Lyten, a maker of lithium-sulfur batteries, said it had bootstrapped enough domestic supplies to have a “tariff-free battery.” [...] While cars of all kinds could get costlier with tariffs, those that run on batteries face more price challenges. Tariffs are highest on China, which automakers and suppliers can’t yet escape as a key source of crucial battery materials. Trade war developments “have put EV manufacturers in a uniquely difficult position,” said Ram Chandrasekaran, an EV analyst at FTI Consulting. “Many will struggle to offset these pressures without eroding already thin margins.”
